chapter_title: Connecting to Wallets and Account Management

screens.title: Connecting to Wallets and Account Management
screens.subtitle: Establishing secure wallet connections, detecting accounts, and handling dynamic changes.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn why connecting a wallet is the gateway to any interactive DApp. A browser wallet such as MetaMask injects a global provider object that represents the user's identity, key manager, and signer. Without a connection, your application is limited to public, read-only blockchain queries. We'll focus on detecting the injected provider, requesting account access via the standardized EIP-1193 request, and keeping the DApp state up to date when the user switches accounts or networks. You will see concrete code patterns for requesting accounts, instantiating a provider and signer with ethers, and adding listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged. We'll also cover practical error handling, what to do when a user rejects a connection, and the minimal security checks you must perform before prompting transactions. By the end of this module you'll be able to reliably connect a wallet, read the connected address and chain ID, and react safely to the most common runtime changes. How will your DApp communicate network expectations to users when they connect?

keyIdea.title: Why wallet connection matters
keyIdea.text: A connected wallet is a user's identity and signing authority. Proper detection, permission requests, and listeners are essential to a safe, dynamic DApp.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Connecting to Wallets
Connecting to Wallets and Account Management
Detect providers, request access, keep the DApp in sync with the user's wallet state.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

A wallet connection upgrades your DApp from passive readers to active participants. The wallet manages keys, signs transactions, and exposes the selected account and network through the standard provider object. This lesson teaches detection, connection, event listening, and safe UX patterns that let your application stay accurate and secure as users interact with their wallets.

In this lesson

  • Detect window.ethereum and request accounts using EIP-1193.
  • Instantiate provider and signer with ethers.js and read chainId.
  • Handle accountsChanged, chainChanged, disconnect, and cleanup.
Why it matters
A connected wallet gives you permission to request signatures and send transactions. It is the bridge between UI intent and blockchain state.
Security focus
Never ask for private keys and never assume the user is on the expected network. Use explicit checks and graceful fallbacks.
Concept Map
window.ethereum
Injected provider (EIP-1193)
eth_requestAccounts
User grants account access
accountsChanged / chainChanged
Keep UI and state in sync
Explore Key Topics
Provider detection: Check typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined' before requesting accounts.
Event listeners: Listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged to avoid stale UI and wrong-network errors.
Security: Never request private keys, handle user rejections, and educate users about phishing and correct URLs.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the role of a Web3 wallet, detect and request account access using the standardized EIP-1193 provider, respond to account and network changes dynamically, and retrieve and present the connected account and chain information. Each objective is practical: you will write code that checks for window. ethereum, triggers eth_requestAccounts, and uses ethers to instantiate a provider and signer. You will also implement event listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged so your UI remains correct when the user switches accounts or networks. Finally, you will understand key security practices to protect users from common pitfalls, such as never asking for private keys and handling user rejection politely. These skills matter because they are the plumbing that connects your DApp UI to real user identity and signing capabilities; without them you cannot safely request or sign transactions. Think about a simple wallet-connected profile area in your app: what should change when the user switches accounts?

screens.title: What is window.ethereum and EIP-1193?
screens.subtitle: Provider basics and the standard that makes wallets interoperable.

narration.text: Let's define window. ethereum and EIP-1193 clearly. window. ethereum is the global provider object injected by browser wallets to expose an A P I for requesting accounts, signing messages, and sending transactions. EIP-1193 is the provider specification that standardizes that JavaScript interface so DApps can interact consistently across wallets. A key claim: treat window. ethereum as an untrusted external A P I — check for its presence, use request method calls, and avoid assumptions about available methods. Concrete example: when MetaMask is installed, it injects window. ethereum and your DApp can call request with method eth_requestAccounts to prompt the user. A common misconception is to assume the provider is always present or that the provider will auto-connect; in practice, users must grant permission and may reject requests. Why this matters: EIP-1193 gives you a predictable set of events and methods such as accountsChanged and chainChanged to react to dynamic changes. Misusing the provider, such as asking for private keys or not handling rejection, compromises security and UX. Takeaway: treat window. ethereum as a standardized bridge and build explicit checks and graceful fallbacks around it. How will you detect absence and inform the user in a friendly way?

keyIdea.title: Provider = bridge
keyIdea.text: window.ethereum following EIP-1193 is the standardized bridge between DApp and wallet; always check presence and handle permission flows.

content.html:
Definition
window.ethereum & EIP-1193
window.ethereum is the injected provider that exposes request-based methods and events. EIP-1193 standardizes this JavaScript API so wallets and DApps can interoperate without bespoke integrations. Treat the provider as a permissioned API you must verify and respect.
Concrete example
If MetaMask is installed it injects window.ethereum. Calling eth_requestAccounts will open a wallet prompt for the user to allow address sharing.
Common misconception
Don’t assume the provider is always present or will auto-connect; user permission is required and may be declined.
Key takeaway
Always check if typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined' and provide clear instructions when absent.
Annotation
Event support is part of the spec. The two most important events you'll use are accountsChanged and chainChanged. These let your DApp respond immediately when the user switches account or network in their wallet, which avoids stale data and incorrect signature contexts.
Quick reference
  • Method calls use window.ethereum.request({ method: '...' }).
  • Events are registered with window.ethereum.on('event', handler).
Key Takeaway

EIP-1193 gives consistent provider methods and events. Use presence checks and explicit user prompts to manage permissions safely.

screens.title: Detecting and Requesting Account Access
screens.subtitle: From provider check to eth_requestAccounts prompt.

narration.text: Detecting a provider and requesting account access is a small but critical process. Start with a simple presence check: if typeof window. ethereum!== 'undefined', a compatible wallet is likely available. The next step is to call window. ethereum. request with method eth_requestAccounts; this triggers the wallet UI and asks the user to grant account access. If approved, the call resolves to an array of addresses. If the user rejects the request, the provider returns an error with code 4001, which you must handle gracefully. A concrete example: call eth_requestAccounts, assign the first returned address as the current account, and then create a provider and signer with ethers. A common mistake is to immediately attempt to sign a transaction without checking that an account exists or without error handling for rejection. Also avoid repeatedly prompting the user; if they reject, update your UI to explain why the connection is needed and let them choose to try again. Takeaway: implement a clear, permission-first flow that checks provider presence, requests access once, handles rejection, and proceeds only when the account is available. What message will you show if the wallet is absent or the user declines?

keyIdea.title: Permission-first flow
keyIdea.text: Check provider presence, request accounts once, and handle user rejection gracefully to preserve trust and avoid repeated prompts.

content.html:
Process
Detect → Request → Resolve
Follow these steps in order to request account access and prepare signer/provider objects for use.
  1. Detect: if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') then proceed.
  2. Request: await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' }).
  3. Resolve: use the returned accounts[0] as the connected address and instantiate provider and signer.
  4. Handle rejection: catch error.code === 4001 and show a friendly explanation; do not re-prompt immediately.
Example result
You receive an accounts array. Use accounts[0] for display and provider.getSigner() for signing operations.
Implementation Pattern
async function connectWallet() {
  if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') {
    try {
      const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
      const currentAccount = accounts[0];
      // instantiate provider and signer with ethers
    } catch (error) {
      if (error.code === 4001) {
        // user rejected request - show friendly message
      } else {
        // handle other errors
      }
    }
  } else {
    // prompt to install a compatible wallet
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Permission must be explicitly granted. Handle rejection and absence with clear, non-blocking guidance.

screens.title: connectWallet Implementation with ethers.js
screens.subtitle: Get provider, signer, account, and chainId from the injected provider.

narration.text: Now let's walk through a concrete implementation of connectWallet using ethers. js patterns included in the chapter. The function first checks for window. ethereum. When present it calls eth_requestAccounts which prompts the user. On success, use new ethers. BrowserProvider(window. ethereum) to create a provider and then call provider. getSigner() to obtain the signer for the selected account. Use provider. getNetwork() to read the chainId and convert it to a string for display. Error handling is essential: handle the user-rejected code 4001 by informing the user rather than repeatedly prompting them. A practical example: after connecting, store currentAccount and currentChainId in state and call setupEventListeners so the app updates on account or network changes. A common misconception is that getSigner always returns a usable signer without verifying the account; verify accounts array before relying on it. Closing question: after the connect step, what state will you persist and when will you call setupEventListeners? connectWallet Implementation with ethers.js means use browserprovider and getsigner to bind the selected account to a signer, and read chainid to validate network expectations.. In practical terms, get provider, signer, account, and chainid from the injected provider.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical connect flow
keyIdea.text: Use BrowserProvider and getSigner to bind the selected account to a signer, and read chainId to validate network expectations.

content.html:
Starter Code
import { ethers } from "ethers";

let provider = null;
let signer = null;
let currentAccount = null;
let currentChainId = null;

async function connectWallet() {
  if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') {
    try {
      const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
      currentAccount = accounts[0];
      provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
      signer = await provider.getSigner();
      const network = await provider.getNetwork();
      currentChainId = network.chainId.toString();
      // setupEventListeners();
      return { account: currentAccount, chainId: currentChainId };
    } catch (error) {
      if (error.code === 4001) {
        // user rejected
      } else {
        // other errors
      }
      return { account: null, chainId: null };
    }
  } else {
    // wallet not detected
    return { account: null, chainId: null };
  }
}
Concrete example
After user approval, currentAccount holds the first returned address and currentChainId is the numeric chain identifier, both usable in UI and validations.
Explanation & Pitfalls
Remember to: verify accounts array length, handle the 4001 error code meaning the user declined to connect, and avoid auto-retrying prompts that annoy users. Use provider.getNetwork() to confirm the network and prompt the user to switch if necessary.
Key Takeaway

Instantiate provider and signer only after a successful accounts response. Then read chainId and initialize event listeners to keep state accurate.

screens.title: Setting Up Event Listeners
screens.subtitle: accountsChanged, chainChanged, disconnect — why they matter and how to use them.

narration.text: Event listeners are how your DApp remains correct when the user modifies wallet state outside your UI. The important events in the provider spec are accountsChanged and chainChanged; many wallets also emit disconnect. When accountsChanged fires with an empty array, treat that as the user locking or disconnecting their wallet and revert UI to a disconnected state. When accountsChanged contains a different address, update currentAccount, re-instantiate the signer, and refresh any account-specific data. When chainChanged fires, the connected network has changed; you should re-initialize contract instances and re-fetch chain-specific data. A common trade-off: some teams call window. location. reload on chain change to guarantee a full re-initialization; this is simple but can feel aggressive. A more graceful approach is to re-fetch contract instances and state based on the new chainId. Concrete example: register window. ethereum. on('accountsChanged', handleAccountsChanged) and remember to remove listeners when the component unmounts. Misconception: listeners are optional — they are not. Without them your UI will show stale addresses or attempt transactions on the wrong chain. Takeaway: add listeners immediately after connecting and remove them on teardown.

keyIdea.title: Listeners keep UI correct
keyIdea.text: accountsChanged and chainChanged are essential to maintain accurate account and network state; missing them leads to stale or incorrect DApp behaviour.

content.html:
Event Setup
Register listeners after connect
Use window.ethereum.on to listen. Typical events: accountsChanged, chainChanged, disconnect. These let you react immediately to user changes rather than waiting for the next action.
accountsChanged
If empty, consider the wallet locked; if different, update signer and account-specific data.
chainChanged
Network changed — reinitialize contracts or prompt the user to switch to the expected network.
disconnect
Reset account, signer, and provider state and show disconnected UI.
Implementation snippet
function setupEventListeners() {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', handleAccountsChanged);
    window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', handleChainChanged);
    window.ethereum.on('disconnect', handleDisconnect);
  }
}

function removeEventListeners() {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    window.ethereum.removeListener('accountsChanged', handleAccountsChanged);
    window.ethereum.removeListener('chainChanged', handleChainChanged);
    window.ethereum.removeListener('disconnect', handleDisconnect);
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Always register and clean up listeners to ensure your DApp stays in sync and avoids memory leaks.

screens.title: Handling accountsChanged
screens.subtitle: Update signer, account state, and the UI when the user switches accounts or disconnects.

narration.text: Handling accountsChanged correctly is essential for user safety and application integrity. The provider emits accountsChanged with the current selected addresses. If the event carries an empty array, interpret that as the user locking their wallet or disconnecting all accounts; you should clear currentAccount and signer and present a disconnected UI. If the first element differs from your stored account, update currentAccount, recreate the signer from the provider, and re-fetch any account-specific data such as balances or allowances. A concrete example: you stored an account and are watching for accountsChanged; when the user selects a different address in MetaMask, your handler sets currentAccount to the new value and calls provider. getSigner() to get the signer bound to that account. A common misconception is to ignore account changes assuming the user will refresh; this will lead to actions being signed by an unexpected account and to confusing UX. Closing question: how will your app indicate to the user that their account changed and that any unsaved actions should be re-confirmed? Handling accountsChanged means when accountschanged fires, clear or update account and signer state and refresh any account-specific views to prevent accidental actions with the wrong identity.. In practical terms, update signer, account state, and the ui when the user switches accounts or disconnects.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Update on switch
keyIdea.text: When accountsChanged fires, clear or update account and signer state and refresh any account-specific views to prevent accidental actions with the wrong identity.

content.html:
Event Handler
What to do on accountsChanged
Key steps: check array length, clear state if empty, update account and signer if different, re-fetch account data, and update UI to reflect the new identity.
Concrete example
If accountsChanged returns ['0xABC...'], set currentAccount to that address, call provider.getSigner(), and refresh balances and allowances tied to that address.
Common mistake
Ignoring account changes or assuming a refresh will occur causes mismatched identities when sending transactions. Always trust the provider event and update state immediately.
Key Takeaway

Treat accountsChanged as authoritative: update signer, clear stale data, and notify the user of any important consequences.

screens.title: Handling chainChanged — reload vs graceful re-init
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs between full page reload and controlled re-initialization.

narration.text: When the user switches networks in their wallet, the provider emits chainChanged. Your application must react because contract addresses, data sources, and expected chain logic usually differ by chainId. There are two common strategies. The simple strategy is to reload the page. Reload guarantees a complete re-initialization of all network-specific objects and removes any stale contract references. The downside is a disruptive user experience and potential loss of unsaved UI state. The graceful strategy is to re-initialize contract instances and re-fetch data based on the new chainId. This preserves UI state and can be smoother, but requires careful code to dispose and rebuild all network-specific resources. A concrete example: upon chainChanged you can set currentChainId to the new value, recreate contract objects with the new chain's addresses or provider configuration, and re-run data queries. A common misconception is believing chainChanged rarely occurs; users frequently switch networks for testing or cost reasons. Takeaway: choose an approach that balances correctness and UX; when in doubt, re-initialize network resources instead of assuming the network hasn't changed. What approach fits your DApp's need for UX continuity versus absolute correctness?

keyIdea.title: Network change strategies
keyIdea.text: Reloading is simple and safe; graceful re-init preserves UX but requires careful resource re-creation for correctness across chains.

content.html:
Option A — Reload
Pros and cons
  • Pros: Simple, guarantees fresh state across the app.
  • Cons: Disruptive, may lose unsaved UI state.
When to use
Small apps or critical correctness needs where preservation of complex UI state is less important.
Option B — Graceful re-init
Pros and cons
  • Pros: Better UX, keeps UI and unsaved state intact.
  • Cons: Requires careful re-creation of contract instances and data flows.
When to use
Applications where a smooth user experience matters and you can reliably re-instantiate network-dependent resources.

screens.title: Disconnect and Cleanup
screens.subtitle: Resetting state and removing listeners to avoid memory leaks and stale references.

narration.text: Disconnect events and proper cleanup are small details that prevent bugs and resource leaks. When a disconnect event happens, clear your provider, signer, and currentAccount variables and show a disconnected UI. In component-based frameworks like React, remove event listeners on unmount to avoid duplicate handlers and memory leaks. The chapter code demonstrates a removeEventListeners function that removes accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect handlers. A common mistake is to forget this cleanup, which results in handlers firing multiple times or referencing stale closures. Concrete example: when your wallet disconnects, set currentAccount to null and provider to null, then display a call-to-action such as "Connect Wallet". Misconception: cleanup is optional because the page will be refreshed — not true for single-page apps where components mount and unmount frequently. Takeaway: always remove listeners in your component cleanup or equivalent application teardown to maintain predictable behavior and memory hygiene. What lifecycle event in your framework will you use to remove listeners? Disconnect and Cleanup means always remove event listeners when components unmount or the app closes to prevent duplicate handlers and memory leaks.. In practical terms, resetting state and removing listeners to avoid memory leaks and stale references.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remove listeners
keyIdea.text: Always remove event listeners when components unmount or the app closes to prevent duplicate handlers and memory leaks.

content.html:
Disconnect
What to reset
Clear currentAccount, signer, and provider. Update UI state to reflect disconnection and prevent accidental transaction attempts.
Concrete example
On disconnect, set currentAccount = null, signer = null, provider = null, and set status to 'Wallet disconnected'.
Cleanup
Remove listeners such as accountsChanged and chainChanged during component unmount or app teardown to avoid duplicate events and stale closures.
function removeEventListeners() {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    window.ethereum.removeListener('accountsChanged', handleAccountsChanged);
    window.ethereum.removeListener('chainChanged', handleChainChanged);
    window.ethereum.removeListener('disconnect', handleDisconnect);
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Remove listeners reliably in your framework's teardown lifecycle to maintain correct event behavior and memory use.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Security Notes
screens.subtitle: User rejection, private keys, phishing, and network mismatches.

narration.text: Security and good UX go hand-in-hand when dealing with wallet connections. Never ask users for their private keys — the wallet is the only safe place for them. If a user rejects a connection, respect the choice; set a clear status message like 'Wallet connection rejected' and allow them to retry intentionally rather than repeatedly prompting. Phishing is a practical risk: always encourage users to verify your DApp's URL, and never attempt to copy wallet behavior. For network mismatches, check the chainId after connection and, when appropriate, call wallet_switchEthereumChain to prompt the user to switch. Do not attempt to change networks silently — the provider request will always require user approval. A common developer mistake is to ignore the absence of window. ethereum — always provide instructions to install a compatible wallet. Another is forgetting to validate chainId before sending transactions, which can cause unexpected failures or costly mistakes. Takeaway: build clear, permission-respecting flows, validate network and account state before sensitive operations, and educate users about safe practices. Which user message will reduce friction and increase trust in your connection flow?

keyIdea.title: Security-first connections
keyIdea.text: Respect user consent, never request private keys, validate chainId, and warn users about phishing to maintain trust and safety.

content.html:
Security Notes
  • Never ask for private keys; wallets protect keys.
  • Handle user rejection (error.code === 4001) with a clear, non-aggressive message.
  • Validate chainId before attempting network-specific transactions.
  • Advise users to verify the DApp URL to avoid phishing.
UX Practices
Provide a clear status area that shows whether the wallet is connected, the current account, and the chainId. If the network is unsupported, prompt the user to switch and explain why. Avoid blocking the user from exploring read-only features when the wallet is not connected.
Key Takeaway

Design permission-friendly flows and validate wallet state before sensitive operations to protect users and avoid errors.

screens.title: React Example: Dynamic Wallet Connection
screens.subtitle: A guided implementation using useState and useEffect (starter code review).

narration.text: This screen walks through the React starter code provided in the chapter. The component keeps account, chainId, and status in state. connectWallet requests accounts and then sets account and chainId based on provider results. Handlers for accountsChanged and chainChanged update state when the user changes wallet configuration. The useEffect hook attempts an initial connect if the wallet is already authorized, registers event listeners, and returns a cleanup function that removes them. Concrete example: when connectWallet receives accounts, setAccount(accounts[0]) and setChainId(network. chainId. toString()) so the UI can display both. A common mistake is to omit dependencies on the handlers in useEffect and accidentally re-register listeners on every render; useCallback and correct dependency arrays avoid that. For verification, run the app locally, click connect, approve in MetaMask, then switch accounts and networks to observe the UI updating. Takeaway: lifecycle management is central — register listeners once, update state on events, and remove listeners on unmount to maintain a stable single-page app experience. What test will you run first to verify your handlers work? React Example: Dynamic Wallet Connection means use useeffect to register listeners and a cleanup function to remove them. avoid duplicate registrations and stale closures with proper dependencies.. In practical terms, a guided implementation using usestate and useeffect (starter code review).. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: React lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Use useEffect to register listeners and a cleanup function to remove them. Avoid duplicate registrations and stale closures with proper dependencies.

content.html:
Starter React Page
'use client';

import { useEffect, useState, useCallback } from 'react';
import { ethers } from 'ethers';

export default function Home() {
  const [account, setAccount] = useState(null);
  const [chainId, setChainId] = useState(null);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('Please connect your wallet.');

  const connectWallet = useCallback(async () => { /* ... */ }, []);
  const handleAccountsChanged = useCallback(async (accounts) => { /* ... */ }, [account]);
  const handleChainChanged = useCallback((hexChainId) => { /* ... */ }, []);

  useEffect(() => { /* attempt connect, register listeners, cleanup */ }, [connectWallet, handleAccountsChanged, handleChainChanged]);

  return (/* UI showing status, account, chainId */);
}
Verification steps
Run locally, connect MetaMask, switch accounts and networks, and observe the connected account and chainId update in the UI.
Common pitfalls in React
  • Re-registering listeners on every render due to missing dependencies.
  • Using stale closures in handlers; prefer useCallback with correct deps.
  • Not cleaning up listeners on unmount.
Key Takeaway

Test dynamic wallet behaviours by switching accounts and networks while the app runs to confirm handlers and cleanup work as intended.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Verify Dynamic Wallet Behaviour
screens.subtitle: Run the provided Next.js page, connect MetaMask, and test account/network changes.

narration.text: This guided activity helps you verify your implementation. Start your dapp with the provided Next. js page. Ensure MetaMask is installed and unlocked. Click the connect action to run eth_requestAccounts. Approve the connection and confirm your DApp displays the connected account and chainId. Next, switch accounts in MetaMask: the accountsChanged handler should update the displayed address and trigger any account-specific refreshes. Then switch networks: the chainChanged handler should update chainId and either prompt a network switch or reinitialize contracts. If the user rejects the connection request, the app should show a clear status message and not retry. A realistic test sequence: connect, switch to a different account, switch to a testnet or mainnet, and finally lock the wallet to observe disconnect behaviour. Common mistakes to watch for are duplicate handlers firing on repeated connects and failing to clear state after a disconnect. After you confirm each behaviour, reflect: did any UI state require manual refresh? If so, consider adding cleanup or more explicit re-initialization steps. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Concise definitions to keep at hand

narration.text: Let's reinforce the six most important concepts from this chapter. First, a Web3 wallet is the user's key manager and signer and is responsible for secure transaction approvals. Second, window. ethereum is the injected provider object that your DApp uses to request accounts and register event listeners. Third, EIP-1193 standardizes the provider A P I so wallets behave consistently for DApps. Fourth, eth_requestAccounts is the method that prompts the user to grant account access. Fifth, accountsChanged notifies your app when the user selects a different address or disconnects, and you must update signer and UI accordingly. Sixth, chainChanged notifies you when the user switches networks and you must re-initialize network-specific resources or prompt the user to switch. Each of these concepts is an actionable rule: check presence, request permission, react to events, and respect user consent. Which of these will you highlight in your app's connection UX?

narration.text: A final set of practice reminders will help you avoid common pitfalls. Always check for the injected provider before requesting accounts. Instantiate provider and signer only after the user grants access. Register accountsChanged and chainChanged to keep the UI in sync and remove those listeners on teardown. Respect the user's choice when they reject a connection request and present helpful, non-invasive guidance. For network mismatches, use the wallet_switchEthereumChain request to prompt a user-controlled network switch rather than attempting to change networks silently. These reminders translate directly into safer code and better user experiences. When you write your next wallet connection flow, review these checkpoints as part of your deployment checklist.
